title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant \(c>0\), all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
definitions: \(U_{n}\) is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output \(f(x)\), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real \(c>0\) there exists \(N(I,c)\) such that the inequality holds for every \(n\ge N(I,c)\). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

importance.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

progress.text: The theory of computational cryptography develops reductions from one-way functions. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby establish equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
Bogdanov and Trevisan give a nonadaptive oracle-reduction barrier to basing average-case NP hardness or one-way security on NP-complete worst-case hardness, unless PH collapses.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.9 explicitly asks whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) implies one-way functions, and separately asks about stronger average-case premises and trapdoor conclusions. This card fixes the basic one-way-function implication.

Liu and Pass strengthen characterizations using boundary hardness of randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Their ordinary deterministic \(K^{t}\) consequence assumes exponential circuit hardness for derandomization; it does not derive one-way functions from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone.

status_note: Explicitly open in the original source. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no derivation of eventually secure classical one-way functions from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone was located. The security quantifiers are stronger than an infinitely-often one-wayness target.

context_blocks.text: If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

sentences: The statement \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) guarantees that some efficiently verifiable problems cannot be solved efficiently on every input.
Cryptographic one-way functions require a stronger kind of difficulty: efficient attackers must fail to invert outputs generated from random inputs.
This project asks whether worst-case hardness alone forces that average-case cryptographic hardness to exist.
A function that is hard only on an extremely rare set would not provide the required security.
Resolving the implication would clarify whether the most familiar complexity assumption already contains the foundations of computational cryptography.
